title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 5
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Fixing the Map
passages.text:
A. For most of the age of sail, a navigator could establish latitude with reasonable confidence and longitude scarcely at all. Latitude follows from the angle of the sun at noon or of a known star, both measurable with instruments that existed for centuries. Longitude has no such direct observable, and the resulting uncertainty was not a minor inconvenience: ships aiming for an island in open ocean could pass it entirely, and coastlines on charts were drawn with confident latitudes and speculative east-west positions.

B. The underlying principle was understood long before it could be applied. Because the earth turns at a steady rate, the difference between local time and the time at a reference place gives the difference in longitude directly. Knowing both simultaneously solves the problem completely. The obstacle was never the theory; it was that no clock existed which could keep reference time on a moving, damp, temperature-varying ship.

C. Two solutions were pursued in parallel for decades, and the rivalry between them is usually simplified into a contest between a lone craftsman and an obstructive establishment. The astronomical method used the moon's position against the stars as a clock in the sky, requiring lengthy observation, published tables and substantial calculation. The mechanical method required a timepiece that would not vary. Both were pursued seriously by competent people, and for much of the period the astronomical approach was the more practical because it needed no instrument that did not yet exist.

D. The mechanical solution, when it arrived, was the product of sustained iteration rather than a single insight. Successive designs addressed the specific ways a clock fails at sea: pendulums are useless on a moving deck, metals expand and contract with temperature, and lubricants thicken. The eventual instruments used balances rather than pendulums, and combinations of metals arranged so that expansion in one compensated for expansion in another. Each was a response to a measured failure rather than an inspiration.

E. Adoption was slower than the technical achievement suggests, for reasons that were rational. Early marine timekeepers were extraordinarily expensive, individually made, and impossible to verify at sea — a navigator could not know whether his instrument had drifted. The astronomical method, though laborious, was self-checking, since an error in observation produced a result inconsistent with subsequent readings. Fleets therefore carried both for many years, using the sky to confirm the clock.

F. The consequence for mapping was immediate and is easy to underestimate. Coastlines that had been positioned by estimation moved, in some cases by hundreds of kilometres, and the shape of the Pacific in particular was substantially redrawn. The improvement was not that new places were discovered; it was that known places were finally located, which mattered more for navigation and for the emerging idea that a map could be a measurement rather than a depiction.

passages.title: What Happened to the High Street
passages.text:
The decline of traditional shopping streets is usually explained by online retail, and the explanation is partly right and chronologically incomplete. In many countries the trend began before internet shopping was significant, and the earlier causes have not gone away simply because a newer one arrived.

Out-of-town retail was the first substantial shift. From the 1970s onward, planning permission for large stores with free parking on cheap land at the edge of towns drew away exactly the trade that town centres depended on: bulky, weekly, car-borne shopping. The high street's disadvantages in that competition were structural rather than commercial — narrow streets, expensive parking, restricted delivery access — and no amount of retailer effort addressed them.

Property economics then locked the decline in place. Retail rents in many jurisdictions are set by valuations that respond slowly to falling trade, and lease terms have historically been long with limited scope for downward adjustment. A landlord holding an empty unit at a high nominal rent may face weaker incentives to let it cheaply than the vacancy would suggest, because doing so re-values the whole holding. The result is a pattern that puzzles observers: streets with visible demand from small independent traders and persistent empty units at the same time.

Taxation compounds it in a way that is frequently raised and rarely resolved. Where business rates are levied on property value, a physical shop carries a cost that a distribution warehouse serving the same customers does not carry to the same degree. This is a genuine asymmetry, though it is often overstated: the tax differential is real and is smaller than the difference in labour and property cost between a town-centre shop and an out-of-town shed.

What has changed most recently is the function of the street rather than its viability. Where centres have recovered, the recovery has generally not come from retail returning. It has come from other uses — food, services, health, leisure, housing above ground-floor level — occupying space that shops vacated. Measured as retail floorspace, these places are still declining; measured as footfall and occupancy, several are not.

This distinction matters for policy because the metric determines the intervention. A programme designed to restore retail will subsidise a use that is contracting for reasons subsidy does not reach. A programme designed around occupancy and movement will support conversions that are already happening, and its main obstacle is regulatory rather than financial: rules written to protect shopping frontages now frequently prevent the changes of use that keep those frontages occupied.

passages.title: How Children Learn to Talk
passages.text:
Every typically developing child acquires a first language without instruction, in roughly the same sequence and on roughly the same timetable, from input that is fragmentary and often ungrammatical. Explaining how has occupied linguistics for seventy years, and the debate has narrowed considerably even where it has not been settled.

The sequence itself is well established and cross-linguistically consistent. Babbling precedes words; single words precede combinations; combinations initially omit function words and inflections. Children then pass through a stage in which they apply regular patterns to irregular forms — producing constructions like "goed" — after having earlier used the correct irregular form. This regression is highly informative: it shows the child is not imitating, since the incorrect form was never heard, but has extracted a rule and is applying it beyond its range.

The classical argument for innate structure rests on what the input lacks. Children reliably arrive at generalisations that the sentences they hear do not uniquely determine, and they do so without the negative evidence that would be needed to rule out alternatives — adults correct meaning far more often than form, and children resist correction of form when it is offered. Something, the argument runs, must constrain which generalisations are considered.

The strongest challenge has come not from denying that constraint but from re-examining the input. Corpus studies of speech directed at children found it more structured, more repetitive and more grammatical than earlier estimates assumed, and computational work has shown that general learning mechanisms extract more from such input than had been thought possible. The dispute has therefore moved: fewer researchers now argue about whether anything is innate, and more argue about how specific to language it is.

Statistical learning has proved to be a large part of the answer. Infants are demonstrably sensitive to the frequency with which sounds follow one another, and can use that sensitivity to identify word boundaries in continuous speech within minutes of exposure to an artificial language. This mechanism is not language-specific — the same infants track statistical patterns in musical tones — which is exactly why the finding matters to the debate.

What remains least explained is the role of interaction. Children learn markedly less from recorded speech than from a person, even with identical linguistic content, and the difference appears to depend on responsiveness: an adult who replies contingently to what the child does produces more learning than one who does not, regardless of how much the adult says. Quantity of input predicts vocabulary less well than the number of conversational exchanges does — a finding with clearer practical implications than most of the theoretical dispute, and one that receives correspondingly less attention.
